payload.question: Do the dynamics of population entropy carry early-warning information about imminent search stagnation in a genetic algorithm, beyond what the fitness history already reveals, and can that signal drive a mutation intervention that recovers faster after the landscape changes?

spec.rationale: Tests three open prediction hypotheses at once with leave-one-landscape-out on the development landscapes. If entropy (H1) beats fitness-only AUROC, it unlocks a held-out confirmatory run and supports B3; if only dispersion/spread help, entropy is not special and the control work should shift to B3d (H7). If none help, the early-warning premise weakens.
spec.title: Dev: entropy vs dispersion vs spread added to fitness (H1-H3)

spec.rationale: Tests whether the B3 stagnation-risk controller shortens recovery after landscape shifts versus the strongest baseline. Win: justifies the full pipeline and a confirmatory run. Loss: the prediction-to-intervention link fails and effort should go to rate/timing checks (H6) or B3d (H7). Included baselines are stall-triggered and hypermutation alternatives.

spec.rationale: Narrow, cheaper test of whether entropy carries information beyond dispersion (fitness+dispersion+entropy vs fitness+dispersion). Positive: entropy has unique signal, supporting the original claim. Negative: entropy is redundant with dispersion, favoring a simpler genotype-dispersion model.

payload.claim: GA adaptively adjusts operator parameters based on individual and population entropy to avoid premature convergence and improve global search capabilities.
payload.source_excerpt: To solve the problem of premature convergence and slow convergence flaws in the traditional genetic algorithm,a new genetic strategy which is based on information entropy is proposed based on analyzing the importance of the diversity.In this strategy,the algorithm will adaptively adjust its operator parameters in accordance with the current individual entropy and the population entropy based on the reserved optimal individual.It organically combines the internal state of population and the genetic operation to guarantee the diversity of the population and improve the global search capabilities
payload.title: An adaptive genetic algorithm based on information entropy
payload.venue: Journal of Zhejiang University of Technology

payload.claim: Shannon entropy can be used as a direct algorithm indicator of population diversity and convergence during algorithm execution.
payload.source_excerpt: Multi-objective optimization inspired on genetic algorithms are population based search methods. The population elements, chromosomes, evolve using inheritance, mutation, selection and crossover mechanisms. The aim of these algorithms is to obtain a representative non-dominated Pareto front from a given problem. Several approaches to study the convergence and performance of algorithm variants have been proposed, particularly by accessing the final population. In this work, a novel approach by analyzing multi-objective algorithm dynamics during the algorithm execution is considered. The results
payload.title: Diversity study of multi-objective genetic algorithm based on Shannon entropy

payload.claim: Genetically encoded, self-adapting mutation rates outperform fixed mutation rates in steady-state GA across diverse NK-landscape test problems.
payload.source_excerpt: This paper investigates the use of genetically encoded mutation rates within a "steady state" genetic algorithm in order to provide a self-adapting mutation mechanism for incremental evolution. One of the outcomes of this work will be a reduction in the number of parameters required to be set by the operator, thus facilitating the transfer of evolutionary computing techniques into an industrial setting. The NK family of landscapes is used to provide a variety of different problems with known statistical features in order to examine the effects of changing various parameters on the performance
payload.title: Self adaptation of mutation rates in a steady state genetic algorithm

payload.claim: Adaptive mutation rate control schemes improve GA performance by allowing the search process to self-optimize mutation parameter values during runtime, freeing users from parameter tuning.
payload.source_excerpt: The adaptation of mutation rate parameter values is important to allow the search process to optimize its performance during run time. In addition, it frees the user of the need to make non-trivial decisions beforehand. Contrary to real vector coded genotypes, for discrete genotypes most users still prefer to use a fixed mutation rate. Here we propose two simple adaptive mutation rate control schemes, and show their feasibility in comparison with a fixed mutation rate, a self-adaptive mutation rate and a deterministically scheduled dynamic mutation rate.
payload.title: Adaptive mutation rate control schemes in genetic algorithms

payload.claim: Memory-based and elitism-based immigrant schemes maintain population diversity while efficiently adapting to environmental changes in dynamic optimization problems.
payload.source_excerpt: In recent years the genetic algorithm community has shown a growing interest in studying dynamic optimization problems. Several approaches have been devised. The random immigrants and memory schemes are two major ones. The random immigrants scheme addresses dynamic environments by maintaining the population diversity while the memory scheme aims to adapt genetic algorithms quickly to new environments by reusing historical information. payload.title: Genetic Algorithms with Memory- and Elitism-Based Immigrants in Dynamic Environments

payload.title: Alternative Splicing in Evolutionary Computation: Adaptation in Dynamic Environments

payload.interpretation: RESULT (development stage, leave-one-landscape-out, 72 test runs, 5186 test points, stagnation prevalence 0.032). AUROC: fitness 0.7475 [0.7005, 0.7949]; fitness+dispersion 0.7731 [0.733, 0.8142]; fitness+entropy 0.8486 [0.823, 0.8746]; fitness+spread 0.7513 [0.7058, 0.7961]. Delta AUROC vs fitness: entropy 0.101 [0.0695, 0.1342] (H1); dispersion 0.0256 [0.0173, 0.0343] (H2); spread 0.0038 [-0.0096, 0.0164] (H3). INTERPRETATION: H1 supported. The lower CI bound (0.0695) is about 7x the 0.01 smallest effect of interest, so this is a large, non-marginal gain. H2 is supported, but the effect is small. The CI excludes 0 and sits above 0.01 (lower bound 0.0173), yet the point estimate is about 2.6 percentage points, and it is about 4x smaller than entropy's. H3 is inconclusive: the CI [-0.0096, 0.0164] spans both zero and the 0.01 threshold, so it neither shows nor rules out a useful effect. Spread is not shown to be a cheap substitute for entropy. Entropy does beat the cheaper no-genotype signal, but only by contrast with an estimated near-zero effect. Note that entropy's advantage over dispersion was not tested directly here. The gap between 0.101 and 0.0256 is suggestive, but the CIs were computed against fitness only. That question belongs to H5. Brier scores barely move (0.0299 -> 0.0291 for entropy), which fits the 3.2% base rate. The AUROC gain is a ranking improvement, and calibration or absolute risk estimates are not meaningfully better. With so few positives, a high AUROC may not translate into useful alarms at an operating threshold. Nothing here speaks to control (H4) because prediction gains do not guarantee better recovery.
threats_to_validity: Development-stage result: the landscapes used for leave-one-landscape-out are the same family used to design features and thresholds, so the estimates are likely optimistic. They need confirmation on held-out landscapes with a distribution shift.

Only 3.2% prevalence of stagnation (about 166 positive points out of 5186 if evenly distributed, but clustered in 72 runs). Test points within a run are autocorrelated, so the effective sample size is closer to the 72 runs than to 5186. The CI width depends on resampling at the run or landscape level, which should be verified. Brier shows negligible improvement, so there is no evidence of better calibration or practical alarm precision.

The entropy-vs-dispersion comparison is untested directly (H5). The 0.101 vs 0.0256 difference cannot be read as entropy beating dispersion until fitness+dispersion+entropy is compared with fitness+dispersion. The entropy features (H_t, dH_t) may also be confounded with feature count or with a stagnation-label definition that correlates with convergence of the population, which would make it partly tautological.

H3 is inconclusive, not null. The CI includes effects above 0.01, so spread cannot be dismissed as a cheaper signal. Also, a prediction gain does not imply a control gain: literature baselines (hypermutation, random immigrants) have not been compared, and H4/H6/H7 remain untested.

payload.decision: Treat H1 and H2 as supported at development stage. Treat H3 as unresolved, not refuted. Next, test H5: does entropy add beyond dispersion?
payload.rationale: E1 results: H1 0.5 -> 0.975 (delta AUROC 0.101, 95% CI [0.0695, 0.1342]). H2 0.5 -> 0.975 (0.0256 [0.0173, 0.0343]). H3 0.5 -> 0.019, status "refuted", but its delta AUROC is 0.0038 [-0.0096, 0.0164]. That CI includes effects above the 0.01 smallest effect of interest, so the data neither show nor rule out a spread effect, and the low posterior comes from the update rule. H4 and H7 moved 0.5 -> 0.49 through coupling and are untested. Entropy and dispersion were each compared only against fitness, never against each other. The result is development-stage and likely optimistic, and Brier barely moves (0.0299 -> 0.0291), so a prediction gain does not yet imply a control gain. H5 decides whether the cheaper dispersion signal is enough and which controller (H4 or H7) to build.

spec.rationale: H5 decides whether the cheaper dispersion signal suffices. Supported (dAUROC CI above 0.01 for fitness+dispersion+entropy vs fitness+dispersion) means entropy is worth keeping and B3 stays a candidate. Null means dispersion is enough and B3d (H7) becomes the controller to build. Larger than the earlier 'small' E3 to resolve a small expected effect.

payload.interpretation:
RESULT (development stage, leave-one-landscape-out, 96 test runs, 6798 test points, stagnation prevalence 0.034). AUROC: fitness 0.769 [0.7365, 0.8028]; fitness+dispersion 0.794 [0.7645, 0.8239]; fitness+dispersion+entropy 0.8625 [0.8386, 0.8857]. H5 contrast (fitness+dispersion+entropy minus fitness+dispersion): delta AUROC 0.0685 [0.0508, 0.0859], standardised effect 0.787. Dispersion alone vs fitness: 0.0251 [0.0177, 0.0325]. Entropy set vs fitness: 0.0936 [0.0697, 0.1179]. Brier: 0.0318 / 0.0316 / 0.0308.
INTERPRETATION: The H5 effect is about 7x the 0.01 smallest effect of interest, and the CI lower bound (0.0508) is also well above 0.01. So within the development landscapes entropy carries ranking information that dispersion does not. This is the first direct entropy-vs-dispersion comparison, and it favours entropy over the cheaper signal. It is a discrimination result only. Calibration barely moves (Brier 0.0316 -> 0.0308, with a 3.4% base rate a constant predictor already scores roughly 0.033), so it does not show that a risk-threshold controller will gain. H4/H6/H7 remain untested; do not carry this to control. Dispersion alone is a small gain (0.0251), so most of the lift comes from entropy.
threats_to_validity: Development-stage only: LOLO over development landscapes, and the same landscapes were used to pick features/designs (E1-E3), so the estimate is likely optimistic; the 0.0685 may shrink on held-out landscapes (confirmatory E6-type test needed, and E6 currently covers only H1/H2, not H5).

Pseudo-replication: 6798 test points come from 96 runs, and points within a run are strongly autocorrelated. The CI is on 96 units and is only trustworthy if it was resampled by run/landscape; with few landscapes in LOLO, between-landscape variance may be understated.

Low base rate (3.4%) means few positive events, so AUROC is noisy and says little about operating-point usefulness; Brier gain is tiny (0.0316 -> 0.0308) and early-warning lead time and false-alarm rate at a usable threshold were not assessed.

Entropy and dispersion are both genotype-based and may be correlated with the stagnation label through shared definitions (e.g., convergence itself), so the gain may be detection of already-ongoing stagnation rather than early warning; the label/horizon leakage was not checked here.

No cheaper-signal comparison beyond dispersion: H3 (fitness spread) is unresolved rather than refuted (CI includes effects above 0.01), and no hypermutation-style baseline trigger was tested, so entropy beating dispersion does not show it beats the best cheap trigger.

payload.decision: H5 is supported at development stage. Move to the control half of the question: test whether the entropy-risk controller beats a rate-matched fixed mutation rate (H6, E5).
payload.rationale: E4: H5 0.5 -> 0.976. Adding entropy to fitness+dispersion gives delta AUROC 0.0685, 95% CI [0.0508, 0.0859]. Dispersion alone adds only 0.0251 [0.0177, 0.0325] over fitness, so entropy carries most of the gain. This favours B3 (entropy) over B3d (dispersion), so H7 is the lower priority. Caveats: development stage only, landscapes reused, possible label leakage, and Brier barely moves (0.0316 -> 0.0308). The prediction half is now well supported, while all control hypotheses are untested (H4 0.49, H6 0.5, H7 0.49). B3 mutated less than B0 in earlier work, so the open control question is timing versus rate, which E5 tests directly.

spec.rationale: One run answers both entropy-controller questions: does B3 beat fixed mutation (H4) and, more sharply, does timing beat rate (H6; B3 mutated ~0.8x of B0). If B3 beats both, entropy-timed control is supported; if B3 beats B0 but not x0.8, the gain is just a lower rate and the entropy signal is not used for control; if neither, the prediction gain does not translate to recovery.

Smaller size and cheaper, no rate-matched arm so cannot settle H6.

payload.justification: E7 is the utility argmax (0.6755). Expected information gain 0.7392 bits, estimated cost 38.21 s of the 1800 s budget, feasible with no violations. It tests H4 and H6 together: whether the entropy-risk controller beats the strongest non-oracle baseline, and whether timing matters beyond the average rate. Both prediction hypotheses are already near 0.975, while the control hypotheses are still near 0.5. The result decides whether the prediction gain turns into faster recovery. Caveat: the control effect size is a pre-registered default prior, not a measurement.

payload.interpretation: RESULT (development stage, 10 seeds, 20 units over ackley and rastrigin). H4 and H6 share one contrast, B3_predictive vs rate-matched B0_fixed_x0.8, and both are inconclusive. The RMST reduction is -1.49 generations, 95% CI [-4.76, 2.2812] (standardised -0.159). The point estimate favours the fixed x0.8 rate (RMST 48.31 vs 49.8 for B3). The CI spans zero and is about 7 generations wide, so it cannot exclude a 1-generation benefit or a 4-generation harm. Smallest effect of interest is 1 generation, so the effect is not distinguishable from the SESOI in either direction. Both B3 and x0.8 beat B0_fixed (RMST 53.78). B3 vs B0: delta RMST -3.98 [-7.4502, -0.73], recovery rate delta 0.2 [0.04, 0.36], Holm reject true. x0.8 vs B0: delta RMST -5.47 [-7.3203, -3.66], recovery rate delta 0.24 [0.15, 0.34], Holm reject true. Recovery rates: B0 0.42 [0.32, 0.52], x0.8 0.66 [0.59, 0.73], B3 0.62 [0.53, 0.71]. Rescue/damage vs B0: B3 rescue 34 / damage 14; x0.8 rescue 32 / damage 8. B3 damages more runs than the cheap constant rate. INTERPRETATION: the gain over B0 is mostly explained by mutating less (mean p_mut 0.1 -> 0.08 for x0.8, 0.0753 for B3), not by entropy-driven timing. The B3-over-B0 improvement is already reproduced by a free, signal-less baseline, which is a comparison where entropy does not beat a cheaper signal. This does not refute H6 or H4; it is merely no evidence of timing value. The earlier prediction-side AUROC gains (E1, E4) have not translated into a control benefit here. CVaR90 is 60.0 for all three controllers, which looks like the censoring cap (tail is uninformative). The H4 comparator is nominally the strongest non-oracle baseline, which here is x0.8 rather than B0, so the H4 contrast is the same underspecified test.
threats_to_validity: Development-stage only, with just 2 landscapes (ackley, rastrigin) and 10 seeds (n_units 20); CI is wide and the result may be optimistic or landscape-specific, with no held-out distribution-shift check.

B3's frozen risk model (fitness+entropy) was fit on only 60 runs and its training landscapes overlap the evaluation ones, so any B3 advantage would be inflated and the null here is conservative; yet B3 still does not beat x0.8.

x0.8 was chosen post hoc to match B3's average rate (0.0753 vs 0.08 are not identical), so the comparison is not exactly rate-matched; also the x0.8 multiplier was not tuned on separate data, and other fixed rates (e.g. x0.75) or hypermutation/random-immigrant baselines were not run.

Recovery time is censored at 60 generations (CVaR90 = 60.0 for all arms), so RMST is truncated, and tail behaviour is invisible; recovery thresholds eps are per-landscape and may favour one controller.

H4 and H6 reuse one contrast and one data set, so the two verdicts are not independent evidence; the rescue/damage counts are paired runs from the same seeds, and McNemar p-values are descriptive only.

payload.decision: Stop at three rounds. The prediction gains from entropy have not turned into a control gain. Next, run a larger timing-vs-rate test with held-out landscapes, a fixed-rate sweep and a hypermutation baseline, plus a B3 vs B3d comparison (E8).
payload.rationale: E7: H4 0.4901 -> 0.3111 and H6 0.5 -> 0.3197, both inconclusive. B3 vs B0_fixed_x0.8 RMST reduction is -1.49 generations, 95% CI [-4.76, 2.2812]. The point estimate favours the fixed rate and the interval spans zero. Both controllers beat B0_fixed (delta RMST: B3 -3.98 [-7.4502, -0.73]; x0.8 -5.47 [-7.3203, -3.66]), so B3's gain is reproduced by a constant rate with no entropy signal. This surprised me. It reopens the assumption that better early-warning AUROC (E1, E4) implies better intervention timing. The AUROC gains are real at development stage, but the controller's benefit looks like a lower mutation rate, not better timing. Caveats: only 2 landscapes, 10 seeds, and a CI about 7 generations wide. x0.8 was chosen post hoc. Recovery is censored at 60 generations, so CVaR90 is uninformative. H4 and H6 share one contrast and are not independent evidence. H7 is untested at 0.49.
